data.hypothesis: The valid 16-row tile was faster on average than the 32- and 8-row variants, but its 32x8 launch still assigns two outputs per Y thread. Keeping the 16-row tile while changing to a 32x4 block tests whether a smaller 128-thread CTA and four outputs per thread improve scheduling or instead make serial work costly. This is a distinct launch-shape experiment; timing benefit is uncertain.

memory_lessons.applicability: This fixed 64-row stencil workload and shared-memory tiling objective.
memory_lessons.claim: Among the measured valid variants, the 16-output-row tile averaged 3.2230 µs, versus 3.3348 µs for 32 rows and 3.3591 µs for 8 rows. The differences come from three samples and do not establish why the variants differ; launch geometry remains a useful independent factor to test.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Hold the 16-row tile fixed and test four Y threads per block against the measured eight-Y-thread shape.

data.notes: The new kernel initializes all 24 shared rows, including halos, before synchronization; each output is covered once and uses the unchanged stencil expression and q<0/q>63 period-63 mapping. No oracle run or new timing is claimed here. The controller should validate signed inputs with independent endpoint values and obtain repeated official full-run timings against the 3.5815 µs baseline and relevant variants.
transformations: Keep the 32-lane contiguous-X shared-memory Y tile and 16 output rows, but change the block shape from 32x8 to 32x4 threads.
Have each of four Y threads cooperatively load six rows, initializing all 24 shared rows, then compute four outputs after the barrier.
Preserve the stencil expression, full output coverage, input and scratch behavior, and wrap only q<0 or q>63 by 63 so in-range index 63 remains distinct.
